title: The Sacred Heart
hookLine: a Friday feast: the heart of Christ as love made visible
tomorrow: The Birth of John the Baptist (24 June)

cards: Above the door of an Irish farmhouse, on a kitchen wall in Manila, on a holy card tucked in a wallet: Jesus, looking straight out, pointing to his own chest, where a heart is shown outside his robe: wrapped in thorns, topped with flames and a small cross, sometimes with a wound in its side.
To anyone who didn't grow up with it, a heart on fire, outside a body, can look strange. For the families who hang it, it's simply part of the house. On a Friday in June, the Church keeps its feast.

teach.b: The heart in that picture starts in John's Gospel, at the cross, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water."
Some early Christian writers saw in that open side the birth of the Church, its sacraments flowing out. Medieval saints, women and men, wrote about resting in the wounded heart of Christ.
Centuries later, in a convent at Paray-le-Monial in France, a nun named Margaret Mary Alacoque reported a series of visions.
In them, Jesus showed her his heart and complained, in her telling, that it had loved people so much and was repaid with coldness. Behold this heart, he said.
He asked for a feast on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi, and for people to receive communion on the first Friday of each month. Her claims met real resistance at first.
It took almost two centuries before Pope Pius IX, in 1856, put the feast on the calendar for the whole Church.
Now it falls on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, which usually lands in June, and June became the month of the Sacred Heart. What's the picture saying?
Catholics read it this way: God's love isn't only an idea.

teach.h: LOVE WITH A PULSE AND WOUNDS.
teach.b: It has a body, a pulse, and wounds. In Matthew, when Jesus speaks of his own heart, he doesn't say mighty.

teach.h: I AM MEEK, AND HUMBLE OF HEART.
teach.b: He says, "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."

how: Catholics keep the solemnity of the Sacred Heart on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, usually in June; many homes display a Sacred Heart image, and some Catholics practice the First Friday devotion of receiving communion on the first Friday of each month.

o: Jesus's heart, honored as love made visible
a heart-shaped relic kept in a Paris church
a vow of love made at a wedding Mass

games.q: you're painting Jesus for a family's kitchen wall. how does the Sacred Heart tradition show his heart?
o: outside his chest, with thorns, flames and a cross.
in his open hands, as an offering.
games.why: outside, wrapped in thorns, topped with flames and a cross, often with a wound. love shown on the outside of the body.

practice: Place one hand flat on your chest and wait until you can feel the beat, a rhythm going since before you were born, without your help. Keep your hand there and think of one person you love who is hard to love right now.
If you pray, you can pray for them, or say Jesus's words, meek and humble of heart; if you don't, feel the beat and wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Sacred Heart. The heart of Jesus, honored as love made visible, wounded and burning. Its feast is a Friday in June, for the whole Church since 1856. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the heart of Jesus, from the feast's name, Sacratissimum Cor Iesu.
